title: Galleon Logistics — SLO sensitivity, multi-tenant routing & fallback evaluation
content:
Executive summary:

This is the solutions-eng POC report for Galleon Logistics (customer). Objective: characterize service-level objective (SLO) sensitivity across a multi-tenant routing configuration and validate automated fallback policies under intermittent capacity degradation. Deliverables: (1) latency and throughput curves for three model variants under representative fleet-routing requests, (2) cost-influence of batching and KV caching for the workload, (3) quantifiable fallback behavior (failover to cheaper model / region / queued mode) and impact on tail latency and error rate, and (4) recommended routing policy defaults for initial production rollout.

Why this POC matters:
- Galleon needs predictable 99th-percentile latencies for live ETA updates and high concurrency for batch planning jobs.
- They will run a multi-tenant setup (internal dispatch + external partner APIs) on a shared Redwood Dedicated pool and expect SLOs to hold even during microbursts.

Test environment and configuration:
- Date range: 2029-10-03 to 2029-10-16 (iterative runs).
- Hardware: Redwood Dedicated 8xA100-80GB equivalents (configured as 4 worker pods, autoscale disabled for deterministic capacity).
- Models evaluated:
  * gln-13B-v1 (quantized, high-throughput profile) — primary cost-efficient variant
  * gln-13B-v1-acc (accelerated attention kernels, slightly higher memory) — target low tail latency
  * gln-70B-slim (floating, higher quality) — fallback for quality-sensitive flows
- Routing policies tested:
  1) strict-latency: prefer low-tail-latency model (gln-13B-v1-acc), cost unconstrained
  2) cost-first: prefer gln-13B-v1 unless p95 > configured SLO then escalate
  3) progressive-fallback: route to cheaper model, then to queued/batched mode under saturation
- Fallback behaviors: immediate model swap, region failover (us-east -> us-west warm pool), queued-mode degrade (return approximate ETA fast + background refinement), and error fallback (500->cached-response).
- Workloads simulated:
  * Live updates: short prompts (~60 tokens) at 250–500 qps steady with 1% spiky bursts (x10) simulating traffic spikes when carriers report events. Latency SLO target: p95 < 150ms, p99 < 350ms.
  * Planning batches: long prompts (~800 tokens) at 10–20 concurrent jobs, throughput-bound, quality-sensitive. SLO: throughput >= 6 jobs/min for baseline batch window.
  * Mixed multi-tenant stream: 70% live, 30% batch with tenant-weighted quotas (internal high-priority tenants get reserved tokens).
- Observability hooks: token-level cost tracing, per-request model version label, KV cache hit/miss ratio, cold-start counts, CPU/GPU utilization.

Key findings (high level):
- Baseline latency (no fallback, no caching):
  * gln-13B-v1: p50=42ms, p95=190ms, p99=420ms at 400 qps steady.
  * gln-13B-v1-acc: p50=35ms, p95=120ms, p99=260ms at 400 qps steady.
  * gln-70B-slim: p50=110ms, p95=420ms, p99=980ms at 400 qps steady.
- Batching gains: enabling adaptive batching with max latency target=80ms increased effective throughput by 2.8x for gln-13B-v1 with median token cost reduced ~34%, but tail p99 increased if batch size exceeded 32 tokens.
- KV/prefix cache: warm-prefix cache for repeated route-context reduced p95 by 25–40% for live updates and lowered token consumption by ~12% across traces.
- Spike behavior and fallbacks: under a 5x spike to 2k qps, strict-latency policy saturated worker queue in ~18s leading to higher queuing latency and stalled batch windows. Progressive-fallback policy activated model downgrade at p95 breach of 200ms and region failover; net result: p95 preserved ~170–210ms but route-level error increased due to short transient (2–3s) of cache miss and cold-region warmup.
- Cost tradeoffs: using gln-13B-v1-acc exclusively would increase monthly token cost estimate by ~42% compared to gln-13B-v1; progressive-fallback realized ~22% cost reduction vs strict-latency with comparable p95 after tuning.

Detailed results (selected charts in attached artifacts):
- Latency curves by QPS for each model variant (attached: pdf latency-curves-test-run-10-12.pdf).
- Tail-latency heatmap across tenant-weight and batch-size sweep (attached: heatmap-coldstart-to-p99-1016.png).
- Cost per 1M tokens extrapolated across month (assumptions included in linked spreadsheet).

Anomalies and notes during runs:
- Region failover warm pool was cold for run on 2029-10-09; first 120s after failover saw 3–4x p99 multiplier due to model cache population. Recommendation: keep minimal warmed replica in failover region for fast handoff.
- Observed mislabeling of a subset of routed requests during A/B policy sweep (github PR-87 fixed a labeling race in router). Ensure canary policy gating for router changes.

Recommendations and action items:
1) Routing defaults for first production rollout: use progressive-fallback with thresholds — p95 threshold 180ms to trigger model downgrade; reserve 25% capacity for high-priority internal tenant traffic; enable prefix caching for live update routes.
2) Warm failover fundamentals: maintain a 1-replica warm pool per region for primary models to limit warmup penalty to <500ms window.
3) Cost control knobs: apply quantized variant (gln-13B-v1) as primary for non-quality-sensitive traffic and enable adaptive batching only for batch routes. Monitor p99 and cap max-batch-size at 32 tokens for live routes.
4) Observability and alerts: emit per-route p95, p99 with automated alerting when p99 rises 30% above baseline; add a synthetic probe that simulates a 10x microburst every 6 hours to validate fallback logic.
5) Next POC iteration: evaluate autoscaling behavior with conservative burstable capacity for 7–14 day window, and run end-to-end experiments with real partner traffic mirror.

Appendix — test plan excerpts:
- Scenario matrix: varied qps (100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000), tenant mix (single-tenant, 90/10, 70/30), batch sizes (8, 16, 32, 64), caching states (cold, warm), failover actions (no-failover, region, model-downgrade, queued-mode).
- Success criteria: maintain p95 <= 180ms for live tier for >= 99% of test windows; batch throughput >= baseline; system recovers to baseline within 30s after microburst with progressive-fallback.

Links to artifacts and raw logs:
- latency-curves-test-run-10-12.pdf (raw charts)
- synthetic-burst-logs-1014.tar.gz (request traces)
- cost-extrapolation-galleon-1016.xlsx
- run-notes and runner config saved in github:solutions/poc-galleon/runs/1010-1016

Open questions for customer workshop:
- Acceptable p99 window for external partner calls (is 500ms tolerable for certain partner SLAs?).
- Risk tolerance for warm failover costs (keep warm pool vs accept brief p99 spike on failover).
- Will Galleon accept model quality regression when downgrading for cost reasons, and how to surface quality degradations to product teams?

Owner and next steps:
- Owner: Aisha Patel (solutions eng lead) — Coordinate a customer-facing workshop 2029-10-22 to review results, confirm SLO thresholds, and schedule the next iteration to exercise autoscaling.
- Engineering follow-ups: Rina Khatri to prototype warm-pool manager (ETA 2029-11-05). Miguel Santos to add synthetic microburst probe and per-route alerting (ETA 2029-10-28). Evan Brooks to draft production runbook for progressive-fallback (ETA 2029-10-30).

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep incremental logs for the billing projection; the spreadsheet assumptions are conservative — run sensitivity +/-15% on token utilization.
- Consider A/B test where partner traffic gets strict-latency lane billed at premium; measure conversion.
